text:
Mashonisas MONEY trap you want to avoid this Xmas
When the money dries up, the mashonisas come out to feed. Here’s how the National Credit Regular (NCR) says you can spot them …
When the money dries up, the mashonisas come out to feed. It is a regular occurrence this time of year, when vulnerable citizens have to extend their finances over the festive season. However, the National Credit Regulator (NCR) warns that economically disadvantaged South Africans need to think carefully before borrowing money from unregistered mashonisas.
The term refers to unregulated money lenders, who promise the world initially but then slowly turn the screws on their victims. Typically, mashonisas profit off excessive fees, high interest rates and other exploitative practices. It’s not uncommon for victims to effectively become hijacked, with the money lenders taking over their bank accounts and more …
AVOID THE MASHONISAS MONEY TRAP
Mashonisas have been known to hijack their victims’ SASSA grant card, bank card and even take their identity documents as a form of collateral. So, the moment money comes into a victim’s account at the start of the month, they withdraw the funds owed – plus an excessive penalty fee – leaving the victim with less and less money.
As such, the South African Police Service (SAPS) claims it is cracking down on illegal microlenders this festive season. But civil advocacy group Soul City warns that Christmas festivities and back-to-school preparations in the New Year can leave many households in financial disarray. Likewise, so does the extended five-week December-to-January pay gap that most salaried workers must endure.
MORE MICROLENDERS IN 2025
However, while taking out a quick loan from the mashonisas might appear to be a lifeline, the Department for Women, Youth and Persons with Disabilities warns that there are many hidden dangers. “The financial exclusion of large sects of society has fuelled the rise in informal lending. We’ve seen a 2% year-on-year increase in mashonisas, with 4 622 operating in the country this year,” says Head of Credit Analytics, Siva Dhever.
Moreover, Dhever says there’s been a 14.5% increase in consumers taking out microloans this year – 3.12 million, up from 2.66 million. Therefore, Dhever says to mitigate against potential mashonisas, borrowers must always verify a lender’s credentials first. Ask the lender for their NCR registration papers. Other red flags include very high interest rates, pressure to sign quickly and demands for unusual collateral (like your SASSA card, bank card or ID document). Don’t agree to this!
But what do you think? Are more South Africans falling foul of mashonisas. Is it because the government simply isn’t providing enough economic opportunity? Be sure to let us know in the comments section below …
